sections.title: Why Impact Weighing Matters
sections.content: In a debate, both sides will present arguments with real consequences. The judge doesn't just count arguments — they decide which arguments matter more. Impact weighing is the skill of proving why your argument's consequences outweigh your opponent's.
bullets: Judges use impact weighing to decide close rounds
Three criteria: Magnitude, Probability, and Scope
You must explicitly compare your impacts to your opponent's — not just list them

sections.title: The Three Criteria
sections.content: When weighing impacts, judges consider three factors:
bullets: Magnitude — How severe is the impact? (Death > injury > discomfort)
Probability — How likely is it to happen? (Certain > probable > possible)
Scope — How many people are affected? (Global > national > local)

sections.title: Weighing Two Impacts
sections.content: Motion: 'This house would ban gasoline cars.'
sections.good: Affirmative: 'Banning gas cars prevents millions of asthma cases in children (scope + magnitude).' This outweighs the Negative's argument about job losses in the oil industry because health impacts affect more people more severely.
sections.explanation: The affirmative wins by comparing: health impacts affect children (vulnerable population), involve serious harm (magnitude), and affect millions (scope). The negative's job loss impact, while real, is smaller in both magnitude and scope.

sections.instruction: Which of the following demonstrates the strongest impact?
options: A policy that might save one person $100
A policy that will certainly prevent 10,000 hospitalizations per year
A policy that could potentially create 50 jobs
A policy that may slightly improve test scores in one school
sections.feedback: Certain prevention of 10,000 hospitalizations has high probability (certain), high magnitude (hospitalization), and significant scope (10,000 people).

sections.q: What is the difference between Magnitude and Scope when weighing impacts?
options: Magnitude is severity; Scope is how many are affected
Magnitude is global; Scope is local
Magnitude is probability; Scope is severity
sections.explain: Magnitude asks 'how bad?' — Scope asks 'how many?' Both matter, and a strong argument scores high on both.

sections.statement: When weighing impacts, you should only focus on your own arguments and ignore your opponent's.
sections.feedback: Effective impact weighing requires comparison — you must show why YOUR impacts are larger, more likely, or broader than your opponent's.

sections.sentence: The three criteria for weighing impacts are {0}, {1}, and Scope.
sections.instruction: Fill in the two missing criteria.
sections.feedback: Magnitude (how severe), Probability (how likely), and Scope (how many affected).

questions.q: Which impact weighing criterion asks 'How many people does this affect?'
questions.feedback: Scope measures the breadth of the impact — from local to global.

questions.scenario: In a debate about banning single-use plastics, the affirmative argues it will save marine life. The negative argues it will cost jobs in the plastics industry.
questions.question: How should the affirmative weigh their impact against the negative's?
options: Ignore the negative's argument and focus only on marine life
Argue that environmental collapse affects everyone permanently (higher scope + magnitude) while job losses can be managed through retraining
Concede that both impacts are equal
questions.feedback: The affirmative compares: environmental damage is irreversible and affects all life on Earth (higher magnitude and scope) vs. manageable economic transition.
